problem: Deductible Amount
solution: Verify claim details and patient demographics. Submit a corrected claim or appeal with necessary supporting medical documentation.
rootCause: The deductible amount has been applied to this claim. This is a Patient Responsibility adjustment, not a denial — the payer has adjudicated the claim and determined that the patient's annual deductible has not yet been met, so the patient owes the deductible portion. The amount shown as the adjustment is the deductible applied; the patient is responsible for paying this amount to the provider. This is a standard cost-sharing mechanism in high-deductible health plans and traditional plans with deductible components.
resolutionSteps: Verify the patient's deductible status on the payer's eligibility portal or via a 270/271 electronic eligibility transaction to confirm the remaining deductible amount.
Check whether the deductible was already met through other claims and the payer's adjudication is outdated; if so, request a claim reconsideration with proof of prior deductible satisfaction.
If the deductible is correctly applied, bill the patient for the deductible amount with a clear explanation of benefits statement showing the payer's adjudication.
Set up a payment plan or offer financial assistance/charity care options if the patient is unable to pay the deductible upfront.
If the patient disputes the deductible or has secondary insurance, coordinate benefits with the secondary payer and submit the claim with the primary EOB attached.
ehrNote: Claim adjusted PR-1 — deductible applied; verified patient deductible status, billed patient for deductible amount, and updated account balance.
preventativeAction: Verify patient deductible status during pre-visit eligibility checks and inform patients of their estimated out-of-pocket responsibility before the encounter to reduce bad debt.

problem: Coinsurance Amount
solution: Verify claim details and patient demographics. Submit a corrected claim or appeal with necessary supporting medical documentation.
rootCause: The coinsurance amount has been applied to this claim. After the deductible is met, the payer adjudicates the claim and applies the patient's coinsurance percentage (commonly 10%, 20%, or 30%) as a Patient Responsibility adjustment. The patient owes this coinsurance amount to the provider. This is a standard cost-sharing mechanism in most commercial health plans and Medicare. The adjustment is informational — the claim is not denied, but the patient balance must be collected.
resolutionSteps: Verify the patient's coinsurance percentage from the eligibility/benefits response (271 transaction) or the payer's member portal to confirm the applied amount is correct.
Cross-check the coinsurance calculation against the allowed amount on the ERA to ensure the payer applied the correct percentage.
Bill the patient for the coinsurance amount with a statement that clearly shows the payer's payment, the allowed amount, and the patient responsibility.
If the patient has secondary insurance, submit the claim to the secondary payer with the primary EOB attached for coordination of benefits.
If the patient disputes the coinsurance or the amount appears incorrect, request a claim reconsideration from the payer with supporting documentation.
ehrNote: Claim adjusted PR-2 — coinsurance applied; verified coinsurance percentage, billed patient for coinsurance amount, and updated account balance.
preventativeAction: Verify coinsurance rates during pre-visit eligibility checks and provide patients with estimated cost-sharing amounts before service to set payment expectations.

problem: Co-payment Amount
solution: Verify claim details and patient demographics. Submit a corrected claim or appeal with necessary supporting medical documentation.

problem: The procedure code is inconsistent with the modifier used.   Usage: Refer to the 835 Healthcare Policy Identification Segment (loop 2110 Service Payment Information REF), if present.
solution: Refer to CPT Code Set: -Add any required modifier(s)
rootCause: The procedure code billed is inconsistent with the modifier used (or missing a required modifier). This commonly occurs when a CPT code requires a specific modifier to convey the clinical context — for example, modifier 25 for a significant, separately identifiable E&M service on the same day as a procedure, modifier 59 to bypass NCCI edits, or modifier 26 for the professional component of a radiology service. The payer's editing logic flags the code-modifier combination as invalid based on CPT guidelines, NCCI procedure-to-modifier rules, or payer-specific modifier policies referenced in the 835 Healthcare Policy Identification Segment.
resolutionSteps: Review the denied line item against the CPT code set and the payer's published modifier policy to determine which modifier is required or which modifier was incorrectly applied.
Access the medical record to confirm the clinical scenario supports the correct modifier (e.g., documentation of a separate E&M visit for modifier 25, or distinct procedures for modifier 59).
Submit a corrected claim with the appropriate modifier added, removed, or replaced, ensuring the documentation supports the billed code-modifier combination.
If the denial was due to an NCCI edit and the services were genuinely distinct, append modifier 59 (or the appropriate X{EPSU} modifier) and include documentation justifying the bypass.
If the payer continues to deny after correction, file an appeal with the operative note or office note, highlighting the clinical rationale for the code-modifier pairing.
ehrNote: Claim denied CO-4 — procedure/modifier mismatch; verified clinical documentation, corrected modifier per CPT/NCCI guidelines, and resubmitted corrected claim.
preventativeAction: Maintain a payer-specific modifier reference matrix and run NCCI edit checks in the practice management system before claim submission; train coders on the top code-modifier combinations that trigger CO-4.

problem: The procedure code/type of bill is inconsistent with the place of service.   Usage: Refer to the 835 Healthcare Policy Identification Segment (loop 2110 Service Payment Information REF), if present.
solution: Refer to CPT Code Set: -Verify Place of Service is allowed for the service(s) rendered
rootCause: The procedure code or type of bill billed is inconsistent with the place of service (POS) reported on the claim. Payers maintain lists of which CPT/HCPCS codes are payable in specific POS settings — for example, an inpatient-only procedure billed with POS 11 (office), or an office visit billed with POS 21 (inpatient hospital). The payer's editing logic cross-references the CPT code against the POS and denies when the combination is not permitted per CPT guidelines, Medicare NCD/LCD policies, or payer-specific POS rules referenced in the 835 Healthcare Policy Identification Segment.
resolutionSteps: Review the denied line item against the CPT code set and the payer's published POS policy to determine whether the procedure is allowed in the billed POS.
Access the medical record to confirm the actual location where the service was rendered and whether the documentation supports the POS billed.
If the POS was entered incorrectly, submit a corrected claim with the accurate POS code that matches the service location and the CPT code requirements.

If the POS is correct but the CPT code is not payable in that setting, determine whether a different CPT code applies to the service as rendered in that location, or whether the service must be billed with a different POS.

If the denial appears erroneous — for example, the CPT code is explicitly allowed in the billed POS per the payer's own policy — file an appeal with the policy citation and the medical record supporting the service location.
ehrNote: Claim denied CO-5 — procedure/POS inconsistency; verified service location in medical record, corrected POS or CPT code, and resubmitted corrected claim.
preventativeAction: Maintain a payer-specific POS-to-CPT compatibility matrix in the practice management system and validate POS against the CPT code at the point of charge entry before claim submission.

problem: The diagnosis is inconsistent with the patient's age.   Usage: Refer to the 835 Healthcare Policy Identification Segment (loop 2110 Service Payment Information REF), if present.
solution: Verify claim details and patient demographics. Submit a corrected claim or appeal with necessary supporting medical documentation.
rootCause: The diagnosis code reported on the claim is inconsistent with the patient's age. The payer's editing logic cross-references the ICD-10-CM diagnosis code against the patient's date of birth and denies claims where the diagnosis is clinically impossible for the patient's age group. Common examples include billing a diagnosis specific to a newborn (e.g., P00-P04) for an adult patient, or a diagnosis specific to advanced age (e.g., M81.0 age-related osteoporosis) for a pediatric patient. This typically results from selecting the wrong diagnosis from the EHR problem list, a data entry error, or an outdated patient demographic record.
resolutionSteps: Verify the patient's date of birth in the practice management system against a government-issued ID or the insurance card to confirm the age on the claim is correct.
Review the medical record to confirm the actual diagnosis documented for the date of service and compare it against the ICD-10-CM code on the claim.

If the diagnosis code was entered incorrectly or the wrong diagnosis was selected from the problem list, correct the ICD-10-CM code to one that is clinically appropriate for the patient's age and the documented condition.
Resubmit the corrected claim with the accurate diagnosis code and the verified patient date of birth.

If the diagnosis is clinically valid for the patient's age but the payer's editing logic flagged it in error, file an appeal with the medical record supporting the diagnosis and a letter explaining the clinical appropriateness.
ehrNote: Claim denied CO-9 — diagnosis/age inconsistency; verified patient DOB, corrected ICD-10-CM code to match documented diagnosis and age, and resubmitted corrected claim.
preventativeAction: Configure the EHR to validate ICD-10-CM diagnosis codes against the patient's age at the point of charge entry and flag age-incompatible diagnoses for coder review before claim release.

problem: The diagnosis is inconsistent with the patient's gender.   Usage: Refer to the 835 Healthcare Policy Identification Segment (loop 2110 Service Payment Information REF), if present.
solution: Verify claim details and patient demographics. Submit a corrected claim or appeal with necessary supporting medical documentation.
rootCause: The diagnosis code reported on the claim is inconsistent with the patient's gender. The payer's editing logic cross-references the ICD-10-CM diagnosis code against the patient's gender on file and denies claims where the diagnosis is clinically impossible for the reported gender. Common examples include billing a prostate-related diagnosis (e.g., N40.0 benign prostatic hyperplasia) for a female patient, or an ovarian diagnosis (e.g., N83.0 ovarian cyst) for a male patient. This typically results from a data entry error, an incorrect patient gender on the demographic record, or a wrong diagnosis selected from the problem list.
resolutionSteps: Verify the patient's gender in the practice management system against the insurance card and a government-issued ID to confirm the gender on the claim is correct.
Review the medical record to confirm the actual diagnosis documented for the date of service and compare it against the ICD-10-CM code on the claim.

If the diagnosis code was entered incorrectly or the wrong diagnosis was selected from the problem list, correct the ICD-10-CM code to one that is clinically appropriate for the patient's gender and the documented condition.
If the patient's gender was incorrectly recorded in the demographic record, update the patient's gender in the practice management system and resubmit the corrected claim.

If the diagnosis is clinically valid but the payer's editing logic flagged it in error (e.g., gender-specific diagnosis in a transgender patient), file an appeal with the medical record and a letter explaining the clinical context.
ehrNote: Claim denied CO-10 — diagnosis/gender inconsistency; verified patient gender, corrected ICD-10-CM code or demographic record, and resubmitted corrected claim.
preventativeAction: Configure the EHR to validate gender-specific ICD-10-CM diagnosis codes against the patient's gender at the point of charge entry and flag mismatches for coder review before claim release.

problem: The diagnosis is inconsistent with the procedure.   Usage: Refer to the 835 Healthcare Policy Identification Segment (loop 2110 Service Payment Information REF), if present.
solution: Verify claim details and patient demographics. Submit a corrected claim or appeal with necessary supporting medical documentation.
rootCause: The diagnosis code reported on the claim is clinically inconsistent with the procedure performed. For example, billing a colonoscopy (CPT 45378) with a diagnosis of otitis media, or a mammogram (77067) with a diagnosis of a fractured ankle. The payer's medical necessity logic compares the ICD-10-CM diagnosis against the CPT/HCPCS procedure and denies when the pairing lacks clinical plausibility. This often stems from data entry errors, wrong diagnosis pointer selection, or failure to link the correct diagnosis to the correct line item.
resolutionSteps: Review the medical record to confirm the actual diagnosis documented for the date of service and the procedure actually performed.
Check the claim to determine whether the diagnosis code was entered incorrectly, the diagnosis pointer was assigned to the wrong line item, or the wrong diagnosis was selected from the problem list.
Correct the diagnosis code(s) to match the documented condition supporting the procedure, ensuring the ICD-10-CM code has the required specificity (laterality, encounter type, severity).
Resubmit the corrected claim with the proper diagnosis-to-procedure linkage, or file an appeal with the office/operative note if the original diagnosis was correct and the denial was erroneous.
If the diagnosis is unusual but clinically valid (e.g., off-label use supported by literature), include a letter of medical necessity with peer-reviewed references.
ehrNote: Claim denied CO-11 — diagnosis/procedure inconsistency; reconciled diagnosis code with documented condition, corrected ICD-10 linkage, and resubmitted corrected claim.
preventativeAction: Configure the EHR to flag low-probability diagnosis-to-procedure pairings at the point of charge entry and require coders to confirm unusual combinations before claim release.

problem: Claim/service lacks information or has submission/billing error(s).   Usage: Do not use this code for claims attachment(s)/other documentation. At least one Remark Code must be provided (may be comprised of either the NCPDP Reject Reason Code, or Remittance Advice Remark Code that is not an ALERT.) Refer to the 835 Healthcare Policy Identification Segment (loop 2110 Service Payment Information REF), if present.
solution: -Verify the procedure code type
rootCause: This denial occurs when the claim or service is missing required information or contains submission/billing errors. The payer expects at least one Remittance Advice Remark Code (RARC) or NCPDP Reject Reason Code to accompany this CARC, identifying the specific missing element. Common causes include missing prior authorization numbers, incomplete patient demographics, absent referring provider NPI, missing or invalid NDC numbers for drugs, or incomplete procedure code descriptions. The vagueness of CO-16 means the billing team must cross-reference the accompanying remark codes to pinpoint the exact deficiency before resubmission.
resolutionSteps: Locate the accompanying Remittance Advice Remark Code (RARC) or NCPDP Reject Reason Code on the ERA/EOB to identify the specific missing or erroneous element.

Pull the original claim from your practice management system and compare each field against payer-specific claim requirements, including any payer bulletins or coverage policies referenced in the 835 Healthcare Policy Identification Segment (loop 2110).

Correct the identified deficiency — add missing modifiers, NDC numbers, prior authorization numbers, referring provider NPI, or any other required data element — and verify the corrected claim passes a payer-specific or clearinghouse claim scrubber before resubmission.
Resubmit the corrected claim electronically with the original claim ID reference and append a cover note (if submitting paper) or 837 transaction note indicating it is a corrected claim.

If the remark code is unclear or the denial appears erroneous, file a formal appeal within the payer's timely filing window (typically 90–180 days) with supporting documentation and a letter explaining the correction.
ehrNote: Claim denied CO-16 — missing/incorrect billing information; identified accompanying RARC, corrected deficient field(s), and resubmitted corrected claim.
preventativeAction: Implement a pre-submission claim scrubber that checks for payer-specific required fields (NPI, NDC, prior auth, modifiers) and run a weekly audit of CO-16 denials to identify recurring missing-data patterns for staff training.

problem: Exact duplicate claim/service   (Use only with Group Code OA except where state workers' compensation regulations requires CO)
solution: -Verify if service was previously billed for the same DOS, billed amount, units/minutes, service code, and/or  performing provider  -If service should be reported for a subsequent time on the same DOS, review and include the appropriate modifier to indicate this is a unique service  -If no changes are to be made to the denied service, this is a valid denial
rootCause: The claim is an exact duplicate of a previously submitted claim for the same date of service, same procedure code, same billed amount, same units, and same performing provider. The payer's duplicate detection logic flags the claim to prevent overpayment. This can occur due to clearinghouse resubmission, manual re-keying, or a practice management system glitch that re-sends claims. Note: CO-18 is used with Group Code OA (or CO where state workers' compensation requires it), distinguishing it from a corrected claim.
resolutionSteps: Search the practice management system and clearinghouse reports for the original claim using the same DOS, CPT, provider, and billed amount to confirm whether the claim was already paid, denied, or is still pending.
If the original claim was paid, write off the duplicate denial — no further action is needed.

If the original claim was denied and this is a corrected resubmission, verify that the corrected claim was submitted with the appropriate frequency code (7 = replacement) and resubmission reference; if not, resubmit as a corrected claim.

If the services were genuinely distinct (same code, same DOS, but separate encounters), append modifier 76 (repeat procedure by same provider) or 77 (repeat by another provider) and resubmit with documentation supporting the separate encounters.
If the duplicate was caused by a clearinghouse or system error, contact the clearinghouse to prevent future duplicate transmissions and document the root cause for your billing team.
ehrNote: Claim denied CO-18 — exact duplicate; verified original claim status, applied modifier 76/77 if distinct encounters, or wrote off as valid duplicate denial.
preventativeAction: Configure the practice management system to flag duplicate claims before submission and establish a clearinghouse reconciliation process to catch duplicate transmissions within 24 hours.

problem: This is a work-related injury/illness and thus the liability of the Worker's Compensation Carrier.
solution: Verify claim details and patient demographics. Submit a corrected claim or appeal with necessary supporting medical documentation.
rootCause: The payer has determined that the injury or illness is work-related and therefore the liability falls under Workers' Compensation rather than the health insurance plan. When a patient presents with an injury that occurred at work or an illness caused by workplace conditions, the payer denies the medical claim and directs the provider to bill the Workers' Compensation carrier. This denial is based on the patient's history, the diagnosis (e.g., occupational injury codes S00-T88 with external cause codes Y92.0 for industrial setting), or information the payer has on file indicating a Workers' Compensation claim exists for this condition.
resolutionSteps: Review the medical record to confirm whether the injury or illness is documented as work-related and whether the patient indicated a Workers' Compensation claim at the time of service.
Obtain the Workers' Compensation carrier information, claim number, and adjuster contact from the patient or employer.
Resubmit the claim to the Workers' Compensation carrier with the WC claim number, employer information, and all clinical documentation related to the work-related injury.

If the injury is not work-related but the payer denied the claim based on incorrect information, file an appeal with documentation from the medical record showing the injury was not work-related and a patient statement confirming the circumstances.
If the patient disputes the work-related designation, coordinate with the patient and employer to resolve the Workers' Compensation claim status before rebilling the health insurance plan.
ehrNote: Claim denied 19 — work-related injury/illness; verified work-related status in medical record, obtained WC carrier info, and resubmitted claim to Workers' Compensation.
preventativeAction: Document the cause of injury and work-relatedness at every visit for injury-related diagnoses and verify Workers' Compensation coverage before billing the health insurance plan.

problem: This care may be covered by another payer per coordination of benefits.
solution: Verify claim details and patient demographics. Submit a corrected claim or appeal with necessary supporting medical documentation.
rootCause: The payer has determined that another payer may be responsible for this claim based on coordination of benefits (COB) rules. This occurs when a patient has coverage under two or more insurance plans and the payer receiving the claim believes it is not the primary payer. Common scenarios include dual commercial coverage, Medicare as secondary with a commercial primary, or active employee coverage that should be primary over retiree coverage. The claim is not denied for medical necessity — it is returned for correct primary/secondary coordination.
resolutionSteps: Verify the patient's insurance coverage on the payer eligibility portal or via a 270/271 transaction to identify all active plans and the coordination of benefits order (primary, secondary, tertiary).

Determine the correct primary payer based on COB rules: birthday rule for dependents with two commercial plans, active employee coverage over retiree coverage, or Medicare Secondary Payer (MSP) rules.
Submit the claim to the correct primary payer first; if the primary has already adjudicated, resubmit to the secondary payer with the primary EOB attached.
If the patient disputes the COB order, obtain a COB letter from both payers confirming the coordination order and resubmit with the documentation.
If the payer that issued the CO-22 is correct as secondary, resubmit the claim with the primary EOB and the correct COB indicator in the 837 transaction.
ehrNote: Claim denied 22 — COB/other payer responsible; verified coordination of benefits order, submitted to correct primary payer, and resubmitted with primary EOB to secondary.
preventativeAction: Verify coordination of benefits order during pre-visit eligibility checks and document the primary/secondary payer hierarchy in the patient record to prevent misdirected claims.

problem: The impact of prior payer(s) adjudication including payments and/or adjustments.   (Use only with Group Code OA)
solution: Verify claim details and patient demographics. Submit a corrected claim or appeal with necessary supporting medical documentation.
rootCause: The adjustment reflects the impact of prior payer adjudication, including payments and/or adjustments already made by another payer. This is used with Group Code OA (Other Adjustment) when coordination of benefits applies — a primary payer has already adjudicated the claim, and the secondary payer is adjusting its payment to account for what the primary has already paid or adjusted. The adjustment is not a denial but a coordination calculation. Common scenarios include Medicare as secondary payer, dual commercial coverage, or workers' compensation coordination. The payer ensures combined payments from all payers do not exceed the total allowed amount.
resolutionSteps: Verify the coordination of benefits order and confirm that the primary payer has already adjudicated the claim; obtain the primary payer's EOB/ERA for reference.

Cross-check the primary payer's payment and adjustment amounts against the secondary payer's adjustment to ensure the combined total does not exceed the allowed amount and no duplicate payments are being made.

If the secondary payer's adjustment appears incorrect — for example, it does not account for the primary's payment or applies the wrong COB calculation — file a claim reconsideration with the primary EOB attached.
Post the adjustment in the practice management system, ensuring the patient balance reflects only the remaining coinsurance, deductible, or copay after both payers have adjudicated.
If the adjustment results in a zero balance and the claim is fully satisfied, close the account; if a patient balance remains, bill the patient with a statement showing both payers' adjudications.
ehrNote: Claim adjusted 23 — prior payer adjudication impact (OA); verified COB calculation against primary EOB, posted secondary adjustment, and reconciled patient balance.
preventativeAction: Always submit primary EOBs with secondary claims and maintain accurate COB records in the practice management system to prevent incorrect coordination adjustments.

problem: Charges are covered under a capitation agreement/managed care plan.
solution: Verify claim details and patient demographics. Submit a corrected claim or appeal with necessary supporting medical documentation.
rootCause: The charges are covered under a capitation agreement or managed care plan. In a capitated arrangement, the provider receives a fixed monthly payment per member (per member per month, PMPM) regardless of the services rendered, and most services are included in the capitation payment. The payer denies the individual claim because the service is already covered under the capitation agreement — the provider cannot bill the payer on a fee-for-service basis for services included in the capitated contract. This is a contractual adjustment, not a denial for medical necessity or eligibility.
resolutionSteps: Review the provider's managed care contract or capitation agreement to confirm whether the specific service billed is included in the capitated services list.
Verify that the patient is enrolled in the capitated plan and that the provider has an active capitation contract with the payer for the date of service.
If the service is included in the capitation agreement, write off the charge as a capitated adjustment — the provider has already been paid through the PMPM capitation payment.

If the service is not included in the capitation list (e.g., a carve-out service like behavioral health or certain procedures), file a claim reconsideration with the contract citation showing the service is separately billable.
If the patient was incorrectly assigned to the capitated plan or the capitation was not in effect for the DOS, contact the payer's provider relations to correct the enrollment and resubmit the claim.
ehrNote: Claim adjusted 24 — charges covered under capitation agreement; verified capitated services list, posted capitation write-off, or filed reconsideration for carve-out services.
preventativeAction: Maintain a current capitated services list for each managed care contract and train billing staff to identify carve-out services that are separately billable outside the capitation payment.

problem: Expenses incurred prior to coverage.
solution: -Verify the Episode is open and active for the DOS billed -Verify Client's eligibility for DOS -Verify the P-AUTH reported is for the correct program, guarantor, and service  -Verify the P-AUTH is active for the DOS billed
rootCause: The expenses or services were incurred prior to the patient's coverage effective date. The payer's eligibility system compares the date of service on the claim to the patient's coverage effective date and denies the claim if the service was rendered before the patient was enrolled in the plan. This commonly occurs when a patient receives services during a coverage transition period, when there is a lag between enrollment and coverage activation, or when the coverage effective date in the payer's system is incorrect. The claim is denied as a contractual obligation — the payer is not responsible for services rendered before the patient was covered.
resolutionSteps: Verify the patient's coverage effective date via a 270/271 eligibility transaction or the payer portal and compare it to the date of service on the claim.

If the coverage effective date in the payer's system is incorrect (e.g., the patient enrolled before the date of service but the system shows a later date), contact the payer's provider relations or member services to correct the enrollment record and resubmit the claim.
If the coverage was genuinely not active on the date of service, determine whether the patient had prior coverage from another payer and submit the claim to that payer.
If the patient had no coverage on the date of service, bill the patient directly or offer financial assistance/charity care options.
If the patient disputes the coverage effective date, obtain a coverage letter from the payer confirming the correct enrollment date and file a claim reconsideration with the documentation.
ehrNote: Claim denied CO-26 — expenses incurred prior to coverage; verified coverage effective date, corrected enrollment if applicable, or billed patient/billed prior payer.
preventativeAction: Verify coverage effective dates during pre-visit eligibility checks and flag services rendered before the effective date for patient financial counseling before claim submission.

problem: Expenses incurred after coverage terminated.
solution: -Verify the Episode is open and active for the DOS billed -Verify Client's eligibility for DOS -Verify the P-AUTH reported is for the correct program, guarantor, and service  -Verify the P-AUTH is active for the DOS billed
rootCause: The expenses or services were incurred after the patient's coverage terminated. The payer's eligibility system compares the date of service on the claim to the patient's coverage termination date and denies the claim if the service was rendered after the coverage ended. This commonly occurs when a patient loses coverage due to job change, plan cancellation, or aging out of a dependent plan, but continues to receive services using the old insurance card. The claim is denied as a contractual obligation — the payer is not responsible for services rendered after the coverage period ended.
resolutionSteps: Verify the patient's coverage termination date via a 270/271 eligibility transaction or the payer portal and compare it to the date of service on the claim.

If the coverage termination date in the payer's system is incorrect (e.g., the patient's coverage was extended but the system shows an earlier termination), contact the payer to correct the enrollment record and resubmit the claim.
If the coverage was genuinely terminated before the date of service, determine whether the patient has new coverage from another payer and submit the claim to that payer.
If the patient has COBRA or continuation coverage, verify the COBRA premium payment status and resubmit the claim with COBRA documentation.
If the patient has no current coverage, bill the patient directly or offer financial assistance/charity care options.
ehrNote: Claim denied CO-27 — expenses incurred after coverage terminated; verified termination date, identified new coverage or COBRA, or billed patient directly.
preventativeAction: Verify active coverage status at every visit via real-time eligibility checks and inform patients of coverage termination before rendering non-emergency services.

problem: The time limit for filing has expired.
solution: -Verify DOS is not more than 400 days (for MH) or 305 days (for SUTS) before bill date for replacement claims  -If bill date and DOS is correct, this is a valid denial
rootCause: The claim was submitted after the payer's timely filing deadline. Most commercial payers require claims to be filed within 90 to 180 days from the date of service, while Medicare allows 365 days (one calendar year). The payer's adjudication system compares the claim submission date to the date of service and denies the claim if the filing window has expired. This often results from claims stuck in a work queue, delayed coding, patient eligibility issues that took time to resolve, or claims lost in a clearinghouse rejection loop.
resolutionSteps: Verify the payer's timely filing deadline from the provider manual or payer contract and calculate the actual filing window from the date of service to the original submission date.

If the claim was submitted within the filing window but the payer incorrectly applied the deadline, gather proof of timely filing — clearinghouse submission reports, 999 acknowledgments, or payer claim receipt confirmations — and file an appeal with this evidence.

If the claim was genuinely filed late, determine the root cause: was it stuck in a coding queue, delayed by eligibility verification, or lost in a clearinghouse rejection? Document the cause for process improvement.

If the payer accepts late claims with good cause (some payers allow exceptions for system outages, natural disasters, or provider-side emergencies), submit a written appeal explaining the extenuating circumstances with supporting documentation.
If the payer will not accept the late claim, write off the balance as a contractual adjustment and implement a timely filing dashboard to prevent future occurrences.
ehrNote: Claim denied CO-29 — timely filing expired; verified submission date against payer filing window, appealed with proof of timely filing, or wrote off as contractual adjustment.
preventativeAction: Implement an automated timely filing alert system in the practice management software that flags claims approaching the 60, 90, and 120-day marks and assigns them to staff for priority resolution.

problem: Patient cannot be identified as our insured.
solution: Refer to CPT Code Set and P-Auth File: -Verify the P-AUTH reported is for the correct program, guarantor (Medi-Cal or County of Santa Clara), and service -Verify there is an open episode for the correct program -Verify client's financial eligibility demographics:        Name        DOB        Address        Coverage effective date        Coverage end date        CIN
rootCause: The patient cannot be identified as the payer's insured member. The payer's eligibility system cannot match the patient's name, member ID, date of birth, or other identifying information on the claim to an enrolled member in their database. This typically results from an incorrect member ID, a misspelled patient name, a name change not updated in the payer system, a transposed digit in the ID number, or the patient is not actually enrolled in this payer's plan. This is a demographic/eligibility mismatch, not a clinical denial.
resolutionSteps: Verify the patient's member ID, name, and date of birth against the insurance card and a government-issued ID to ensure the claim was submitted with the correct demographic information.
Run a 270/271 eligibility transaction with the exact member ID and name to confirm the patient is enrolled and identify any demographic discrepancies in the payer's system.
If the member ID or name was entered incorrectly on the claim, correct the information in the practice management system and resubmit the claim with the accurate member ID and patient demographics.
If the patient's name changed (e.g., marriage, divorce), contact the payer to update the enrollment record and resubmit once the payer confirms the update.

rootCause: The patient has reached the lifetime benefit maximum under their insurance plan. Some plans impose a lifetime cap on certain benefits — most commonly mental health, substance abuse, rehabilitation, or transplant services — after which no further benefits are payable for that category. Note that the Affordable Care Act (ACA) eliminated lifetime limits on essential health benefits for most plans, but grandfathered plans, certain non-essential benefits, and self-funded plans may still have lifetime caps in effect.
resolutionSteps: Verify the patient's lifetime benefit maximum status by contacting the payer's provider relations or checking the payer portal for the accumulated benefit usage and the remaining balance.

If the lifetime maximum has been reached and the plan is ACA-compliant for essential health benefits, file an appeal citing the ACA prohibition on lifetime limits for essential health benefits.

If the lifetime maximum is valid (e.g., non-essential benefit, grandfathered plan), determine whether the patient has secondary insurance that may cover the service and submit the claim with the primary EOB.
If no other coverage is available, bill the patient directly or offer financial assistance/charity care options for the non-covered service.

resolutionSteps: Obtain the payer's authorization denial letter or portal notification to understand the specific reason the authorization was denied (medical necessity, non-covered benefit, or plan exclusion).
Review the payer's coverage policy or medical necessity criteria for the denied service to identify what documentation or criteria were not met.

If the service was not yet rendered, inform the patient of the authorization denial and discuss alternative treatment options or the option to proceed as a self-pay service with a signed financial responsibility form.
If the service was already rendered, file a formal appeal with a detailed letter of medical necessity, the complete clinical documentation, and references to the payer's policy criteria that are met.

rootCause: The service was denied because it is a routine/preventive exam or a diagnostic/screening procedure performed in conjunction with a routine/preventive exam, and the patient's plan does not cover routine preventive services. When a preventive service is billed, the payer denies it as non-covered. If a diagnostic or screening procedure was performed during the same visit as a routine exam, the payer may bundle the diagnostic service with the non-covered routine exam and deny both.
resolutionSteps: Review the medical record to determine whether the visit was a routine/preventive exam or a problem-oriented visit with a specific chief complaint and medical necessity.
If the visit was problem-oriented (not routine), correct the E&M code and diagnosis codes to reflect the medical necessity of the visit and resubmit the claim with the supporting documentation.

If the visit was routine/preventive, verify whether the patient's plan covers preventive services under the ACA essential health benefits; if the plan is ACA-compliant, file an appeal citing the ACA preventive services coverage requirement.
If the plan genuinely excludes routine preventive services, determine whether the patient signed a financial responsibility form or ABN acknowledging non-coverage; if so, bill the patient.

problem: These are non-covered services because this is not deemed a 'medical necessity' by the payer.   Usage: Refer to the 835 Healthcare Policy Identification Segment (loop 2110 Service Payment Information REF), if present.
solution: Verify claim details and patient demographics. Submit a corrected claim or appeal with necessary supporting medical documentation.
rootCause: The service was denied because the payer determined it is not medically necessary based on the patient's diagnosis, clinical history, or the service itself. Medical necessity denials are among the most common and contestable denials — the payer applies coverage policy criteria (e.g., NCD/LCD for Medicare, clinical policies for commercial payers) to determine whether the service was reasonable and necessary for the documented condition. Common triggers include screening services billed as diagnostic, procedures without supporting documentation, or services outside the payer's coverage policy.
resolutionSteps: Obtain the payer's medical necessity policy (NCD/LCD for Medicare, clinical policy for commercial) for the denied CPT/HCPCS code to understand the specific criteria the payer applied.
Review the medical record thoroughly — office notes, operative notes, lab results, imaging reports — to identify documentation that supports medical necessity per the payer's policy criteria.

If the documentation supports medical necessity, file a formal appeal with a detailed letter of medical necessity, the relevant clinical documentation, and references to the payer's own policy criteria that are met.

If the documentation is insufficient, determine whether additional documentation can be obtained from the provider; if not, consider whether the service can be rebilled with a different diagnosis that meets medical necessity criteria.

If the appeal is denied, escalate to the second level of appeal (independent review organization for Medicare, external review for commercial) with peer-reviewed literature supporting the medical necessity of the service.
ehrNote: Claim denied 50 — not medically necessary; reviewed payer medical necessity policy, gathered supporting clinical documentation, and filed appeal with letter of medical necessity.
preventativeAction: Implement a pre-authorization or pre-determination process for services commonly denied for medical necessity, and train providers to document the clinical rationale that maps to payer medical necessity criteria at the point of care.

rootCause: The procedure, treatment, or drug was denied because the payer deemed it experimental or investigational. Payers maintain clinical policies and formularies that classify services as experimental, investigational, or not yet proven effective based on clinical evidence, FDA approval status, and professional society guidelines. Common examples include off-label drug use, emerging surgical techniques, clinical trial interventions, and high-cost specialty drugs not yet on the payer's formulary. The payer applies these policies to deny services that lack sufficient evidence of efficacy, even if the provider believes the service is medically necessary.
resolutionSteps: Obtain the payer's clinical policy or formulary document for the denied service to understand the specific criteria used to classify it as experimental or investigational.

File a formal appeal with a detailed letter of medical necessity, the clinical evidence, and references to the payer's own policy criteria that may be met with additional documentation.
If the service is part of an FDA-approved clinical trial, include the trial registration and protocol documentation to support the appeal.

If the appeal is denied, escalate to external review (independent review organization) where an independent clinical reviewer assesses the medical necessity and experimental designation; many states require payers to honor external review decisions.

rootCause: The claim was processed based on multiple or concurrent procedure rules. This is an adjustment, not a denial — the payer applied bundling or multiple-procedure payment rules to the claim. Common scenarios include multiple surgery rules (where the most complex procedure is paid at 100% and subsequent procedures are paid at 50%), concurrent anesthesia rules, or diagnostic imaging payment rules. resolutionSteps: Review the ERA/EOB to understand which multiple-procedure rule was applied (multiple surgery, concurrent anesthesia, diagnostic imaging) and which procedures were affected by the payment reduction.

Cross-check the multiple-procedure reduction calculation against the payer's published payment rules to ensure the correct percentage was applied to the correct procedures.

rootCause: The payer deems the information submitted on the claim does not support the level of service billed. This is similar to CO-151 but is used as a denial rather than an adjustment — the payer has reviewed the documentation (either pre-payment or post-payment) and determined that the billed E&M level or procedure code is not supported by the documentation. Common examples include billing a 99214 (level 4 established patient) when the documentation supports only a 99213 (level 3), or billing a comprehensive procedure code when the documentation supports only a limited code. The payer may downcode the service or deny it entirely.
resolutionSteps: Obtain the payer's review findings or the RARC that explains why the submitted documentation does not support the billed level of service.

Review the medical record against the documentation guidelines for the billed code (1995/1997 E&M guidelines, MDM table, or CPT code-specific documentation requirements) to assess whether the documentation supports the billed level.
If the documentation supports the original level, file a formal appeal with the complete medical record, a coding rationale letter, and references to the applicable documentation guidelines.

If the documentation does not support the original level, accept the payer's determination, post the adjusted payment if one was made, and educate the provider on documentation requirements to prevent future downcoding.

If the payer denied the claim entirely rather than downcoding it, determine whether a corrected claim with a lower-level code is appropriate or whether the appeal should proceed with the original code.
ehrNote: Claim denied 150 — documentation does not support service level; reviewed against E&M/CPT guidelines, appealed if supported, or accepted downcode and educated provider.
preventativeAction: Conduct quarterly internal E&M coding audits using certified coders, provide documentation feedback to providers, and implement EHR-based coding calculators that suggest the appropriate level based on documented MDM.

rootCause: The claim was denied because precertification, authorization, notification, or pre-treatment was absent. The payer requires prior authorization for certain services (e.g., advanced imaging, surgeries, specialty drugs, durable medical equipment) and the claim was submitted without evidence that authorization was obtained. This is one of the most preventable denials — it occurs when the front office or clinical staff fails to initiate the authorization process before the service is rendered, or the authorization was obtained but not linked to the claim.
resolutionSteps: Check the practice management system and payer portal to determine whether a prior authorization was obtained for this service and date of service; if it was, verify the authorization number was entered on the claim.

If no authorization was obtained, contact the payer immediately to request retro-authorization; some payers allow retro-authorization within a limited window (typically 14–30 days) if the service was medically necessary.

If retro-authorization is denied, file a formal appeal with a letter of medical necessity, the clinical documentation supporting the service, and an explanation of the administrative error that caused the missing authorization.

If the authorization was obtained but not linked to the claim, resubmit the corrected claim with the authorization number in the appropriate 837 loop (2300 REF*G1 for institutional, 2300/2400 REF*G1 for professional).
If the payer will not overturn the denial, write off the balance as a provider write-off (if in-network) or bill the patient (if out-of-network and permitted by the plan).
ehrNote: Claim denied CO-197 — prior authorization absent; verified authorization status, requested retro-auth if applicable, or appealed with medical necessity documentation.
preventativeAction: Maintain a payer-specific prior authorization list in the practice management system with automated alerts for services requiring authorization, and require front-office staff to confirm authorization before scheduling any procedure.

rootCause: The precertification, notification, authorization, or pre-treatment that was obtained exceeded the approved limits. Unlike CO-197 (where authorization was absent), CO-198 means an authorization was obtained but the service rendered exceeded the scope of what was authorized — for example, more units were billed than authorized, the service was rendered on a date outside the authorization date range, or the procedure performed was beyond what the authorization covered. The payer's system cross-references the authorized units, date range, and CPT codes against the claim and denies the portion that exceeds the authorization.
resolutionSteps: Verify the authorization details — approved units, date range, and covered CPT codes — by checking the payer portal or the authorization approval letter.
Compare the authorized units and date range against the services billed on the claim to identify the specific discrepancy (extra units, out-of-range date, or unauthorized procedure).

If the service genuinely exceeded the authorization (e.g., additional units were medically necessary), request an authorization amendment or additional authorization from the payer with clinical justification for the additional services.

If the authorization was incorrectly applied — for example, the units were within the authorized limit but the payer's system miscounted — file a claim reconsideration with the authorization approval documentation showing the correct unit count.
If the authorization cannot be extended and the appeal is denied, write off the non-authorized portion as a provider adjustment or bill the patient if permitted by the plan.
ehrNote: Claim denied 198 — authorization exceeded; verified authorized units/date range, requested authorization amendment for additional services, or filed reconsideration for miscounted units.
preventativeAction: Track authorized units and date ranges in the practice management system and alert clinical staff when a patient is approaching the authorization limit so an extension can be requested before the service is rendered.

rootCause: The service, equipment, or drug is not covered under the patient's current benefit plan. This is a plan-level exclusion — the service may be covered under a different plan tier or a different payer, but the patient's current plan does not include it as a benefit. If the service is genuinely excluded, determine whether the patient signed an Advance Beneficiary Notice (ABN) or financial responsibility form; if so, bill the patient for the non-covered amount.

rootCause: The referral was exceeded — the patient has used up the number of visits or services authorized under the referral from their primary care physician (PCP). This is common in HMO plans where a PCP referral is required for specialist visits, and the referral specifies a limited number of visits (e.g., 3 visits, 6 months). Once the authorized visits are exhausted, the payer denies subsequent claims with CO-287. This is an administrative denial, not a clinical one — the services may have been medically necessary, but the referral limit was reached.
resolutionSteps: Verify the referral details — number of visits authorized, date range, and visits already used — by contacting the PCP office or checking the payer portal.
If the referral was exceeded due to additional medically necessary visits, request a new or extended referral from the PCP with clinical justification for the additional visits.
If the referral was exceeded but the services were urgent or emergent, file an appeal with documentation of the clinical urgency and the medical necessity of the additional visits.
If the referral was not actually exceeded (e.g., the payer's visit count is incorrect), provide the referral documentation and visit history to the payer and request a claim reconsideration.
If the referral cannot be extended and the appeal is denied, determine whether the patient can be billed per the plan's provisions or whether the balance must be written off as a provider adjustment.
ehrNote: Claim denied 287 — referral exceeded; verified referral visit limits, requested extended referral from PCP if medically necessary, or appealed with clinical documentation.
preventativeAction: Track referral visit counts in the practice management system and alert front-office staff when a patient is approaching the referral limit so a new referral can be obtained before the next visit.
